sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: With model weights fixed, we measure how much of an entity-replacement response transfers between English factual questions, beyond whether answers change. We add the hidden-state change from two source questions to a target question about the same entity, comparing the predicted log-probability shift between two relations' published answers, given known answer prefixes, with the measured one. Hidden reuse injects the aligned change at 50% depth before the target's remaining layers; direct reuse adds source output-score changes. With other-relation sources, hidden reuse removes 45% and 49% of no-change error on 0.5-1B Qwen and Llama. Gemma-2-2B removes 22% and passes one of three comparisons in plain text without its default beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token. A later protocol restoring it yields 58-68%, passing every comparison on three cohorts. Larger checkpoints, chat format and new entities show replication and format- or cohort-dependent failures. On small plain-format checkpoints, other-relation hidden reuse mainly reproduces the shift both relations' questions share, without reliably lowering relation-selective error. With target-relation sources, hidden reuse's post hoc advantage over direct reuse is 0.2-0.9 nats outside chat format, unconfirmed and not replacement-specific. The same relation-neutral change at both questions' entity tokens lowers relation-selective error more than random or other-replacement changes, indicating receiving-question dependence.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Steering and function vectors reuse recorded activation changes across prompts (Turner et al., 2024; Panickssery et al., 2024; Todd et al., 2024). Accounts of factual recall likewise predict that mid-depth changes at an entitys tokens can be read out by another questions later layers (Geva et al., 2023; Nanda et al., 2023). changed answer, however, does not tell us how much of the receiving questions response has been reproduced. Entity replacement makes that reference measurable: we can replace the entity in the receiving question itself, which we call the target, and compare its actual response with the transferred one. How faithfully can response recorded in one question reproduce the response in another, and does the transfer also reproduce the part of that response specific to the relation each question asks about? An entity-replacement response is the hidden-state or output-score change caused by replacing the named entity. We measure its reproduction in answer scores. Replacing SLIB with JDeveloper in question about SLIBs developer shifts the log probability of JDevelopers published developer answer, Oracle Corporation, against its programming-language answer, Java; each answer is scored as complete string, token by token after its known preceding tokens. The question about the programming language scores the same answers in the opposite order. shift toward Oracle Corporation in both questions is shared; shift of each question toward its own relations answer is relation-selective (Section 3). Overall fidelity concerns the full measured contrast change. Each prediction is compared with predicting no change and with transferring different replacements response. sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Cross-prompt reuse of recorded changes. Activation addition and contrastive activation addition transfer promptpair differences (Turner et al., 2024; Panickssery et al., 2024), and representation engineering and inference-time intervention shift activations along directions estimated from many examples (Zou et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023); function, task, binding and relation vectors transfer recorded states, function vectors acting when added at early and middle layers (Todd et al., 2024; Hendel et al., 2023; Feng and Steinhardt, 2024; Wang et al., 2024). Request patching distinguishes receiving-prompt computation at middle layers from donor-output copying at late layers (Variengien and Winsor, 2025). States mapped between prompt conditions recover target-prompt behavior (Cheng and Kriegeskorte, 2026); concepts patched across translation prompts are read out in the receiving language (Dumas et al., 2025). Entity representations also transfer across queries. RAVEL interchanges entity representations between prompts about different attributes or from generic sentences about the entity (Huang et al., 2024), and Patchscopes and related methods decode subject and other hidden states in other prompts (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024; Pal et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024). REMEDI adds learned edits to entity representations to change downstream generation (Hernandez et al., 2024). Wang and Xu (2025) find that subject-representation interchange, including from prompts about another relation, largely matches textual substitution in answer agreement and probabilities, with subject effects in early and middle layers. Their measures differ from ours, the share of the targets own signed contrast change that is reproduced, so the two results are not directly comparable; Section 4.3 compares state replacement with additive entity-row patches under our measure. Knowledge-editing evaluations ask whether an edited fact generalizes to paraphrases (Meng et al., 2023) and related facts (Cohen et al., 2024). We instead measure how much of replacements signed complete-answer change transfers additively across questions and separate shared from relation-selective components. Mean-centering improves steering vectors (Jorgensen et al., 2023), and steering evaluations study reliability and context dependence (Tan et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2025). Interventions and factual recall. Causal mediation studies internal pathways, including gender bias (Vig et al., 2020); causal tracing localizes factual associations (Meng et al., 2022), though localization need not indicate where edits work best (Hase et al., 2023). Causal abstraction formalizes interchange interventions, also on learned subspaces (Geiger et al., 2021, 2024, 2025). Factual recall enriches subjects before extracting attributes (Geva et al., 2023). Subject lookups do not depend on the preceding context (Nanda et al., 2023), and both relation-agnostic subject heads and relation-specific components contribute additive updates (Chughtai et al., 2024; Merullo et al., 2024). Multi-token names may form implicit vocabulary items (Feucht et al., 2024), and heads favoring memorized or in-context answers compete and can be rescaled (Yu et al., 2023; Ortu et al., 2024). Lindsey et al. (2025) insert California features recorded in another prompt into Dallas prompt, eliciting Sacramento; Agarwal (2026) finds entity-token patches effective in early and middle layers and final-token patches only in late layers. These accounts predict the mid-depth transfer whose fidelity we quantify. Zhang and Nanda (2024) and Heimersheim and Nanda (2024) discuss patching metrics and interpretation; our equal-length edits follow the formers symmetric token replacement. Alternative pathways (Makelov et al., 2024) and token entrainment (Niu et al., 2025) complicate mechanistic interpretations of agreement. Interventions can produce off-distribution representations (Grant et al., 2025); Perturbations and content controls. random norm-matched vectors can shift distributions more than steering vectors (Turner et al., 2024, App. G), and content-free directions move behaviors similarly (Malla et al., 2026), which motivates different-replacement and random controls. Complementary work uses stepwise distributional change and uncertainty to diagnose reasoning failures (Chen et al., 2026); we measure the fidelity of replacement-induced changes transferred across questions.

sections.title: 3 Setting and Response Comparisons
sections.content: Materials and models. relation is the queried attribute, and template is its wording with an entity slot. ZsRE, zero-shot relation extraction dataset, supplies published factual questions, answers and exact relation labels (Levy et al., 2017). Each block crosses two entity replacements with two relations, each with two source questions and one target question; within each cohort, relation labels, entities, known aliases, templates and complete inputs are disjoint across blocks, and selection uses factual records, Wikidata entity identities and aliases (Vrandeˇcic and Krötzsch, 2014) and the tokenizers, before any model outputs were measured. Table 1 lists the studies, Appendix B.4 four earlier next-token studies, and Appendix eligibility, overlap and study order. The answer results use three cohorts of new-entity blocks whose relation labels and templates mostly recur from earlier studies (Appendix B.2): the original cohort of 35 blocks (140 targets) and two fresh cohorts of 33 and 31 blocks; pooled analyses use all 99 blocks. The earlier 40-block crossing cohort supplies the example of Figure 1, earlier next-token tests and the descriptive comparison that motivated other-relation sources (Appendices B.1, B.4 and B.5). 3 Cross-Prompt Response Reuse PREPRINT We use released Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024), Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (Meta, 2024) and Gemma-2-2Bit (Gemma Team, 2024), with same-family 7B, 8B and 9B replications. Changes are injected at an interface, the hidden state at decoder-layer boundary; confirmatory interventions use the interface at 50% depth. Models run deterministically on CPU in float32; construction and scoring use float64. Determinism here holds for fixed inputs and batch shapes. The plain format, fixed by the original protocol before outcomes, omits chat templates and the default Llama/Gemma BOS token. Later protocols compare chat format and plain text with only BOS restored (plain+BOS). The depth scan and the later testbed, read-out, steering-completion and identical-content studies use each checkpoints default encoding: plain for Qwen, whose tokenizer adds no BOS, and plain+BOS for Llama and Gemma. Appendix B.3 gives the exact checkpoints, interfaces and input formats.

sections.title: 4.2 Depth and row position of answer reuse
sections.content: We next ask where in the target computation these responses remain reusable. pre-specified descriptive scan injects the same responses at nine interfaces from the decoder input (d = 0) to the last layer (d = 1), keeping the source weights from 50% depth. Span-aligned addition copies the changed entity span tokenwise, interpolates only the later question and cue rows, and copies answer-prefix rows. At each replacement endpoint, changed-span token IDs match across source and target questions, so at = 0 it reproduces the edited target by construction. Row subsets separate entity rows from post-entity question, cue and answer-prefix rows. Oracle patches add the targets own edited-minus-clean states to the same rows (Appendix E). In each checkpoints default encoding the share removed by span-aligned addition declines with depth on every checkpoint, from 100% at = 0 to 4670% at = 1/2 (Figure 2). Up to 50% depth, transferred entity rows remove somewhat less error than the targets own entity-row patch  (Table 26)  . With target-relation sources, all aligned rows remove more error than entity rows alone at = 1/2, with pointwise intervals excluding zero on all five checkpoints with these runs  (Table 27)  . At = 7/8 the targets own post-entity change removes most of the no-change error, 8 Cross-Prompt Response Reuse PREPRINT but other-relation responses on those rows remove far less  (Table 26)  . Row effects are not additive: at = 1/2, the targets own entity-row and post-entity-row changes, continued separately and added as predicted contrast changes, remove 4969% of the no-change error, whereas patching both together reproduces the edit (Appendix E). Omitting answer-prefix rows keeps most of the span-aligned share at = 1/2 (Tables 26 and 27), so under candidate scoring one question-plus-cue capture carries most of this gain.

sections.title: 4.3 Standard constructions on the testbed
sections.content: Using the same answer-error reference, we ask whether single vector can substitute for the aligned change matrix. The testbed protocol compares standard constructions over the 99 blocks at the 1/2 interface in default encoding. Its simplest single vector is the weighted source change at the last entity row, kept at its native scale and added at every target row from the entity onward; contrastive activation addition instead starts after the prompt (Panickssery et al., 2024). This broadcast vector has larger mean error than zero prediction on all six checkpoints (Table 16c), and span-aligned addition beats it in 9599 blocks  (Table 30)  . At matched entity-row coverage, span-aligned changes lower error by 0.300.49 nats relative to native-scale vector (descriptive; Table 16c). Entity-state replacement (Huang et al., 2024; Wang and Xu, 2025) and additive entity-row patches differ by 0.06 to 0.01 nats, undistinguished by the pre-specified tests. Span-aligned addition also lowers mean error relative to the confirmatory suffix interpolation by 0.120.28 nats, with all six pointwise intervals excluding zero (descriptive; Table 16c). Two protocols then tuned single vectors on the original cohort and tested them on the two fresh cohorts, which earlier studies had already used (64 blocks). The testbeds tuned comparison (D1c in Table 30) selects the coefficient of one last-entity-row vector added at each entity row, without broadcasting it to later rows. The later steering-completion protocol of Table 1 selects the best of 90 constructions by minimizing mean block answer error on the original cohort; they vary averaging (single-pair or sixteen-context), direction (entity or answer cue), placement and amplitude  (Table 3)  . After tuning, the broadcast vectors pre-specified test against zero passes on three checkpoints, one under pooled correction. Rowwise norm matching scales one direction to the span-aligned row norms and beats zero on five checkpoints over all 99 blocks, four under pooled correction. Sixteen-context averaging gives no detected gain in its pre-specified comparison. Span-aligned addition beats the best of the 90 constructions (a norm-matched direction on four checkpoints) on all but Llama-3.1-8B under family-wise correction and on four under pooled correction; two of the five passes repeat earlier tests (Appendix F).

sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: What the quantitative profile adds. For reuse of recorded changes, overall fidelity and relation selectivity can diverge: measured against the targets own response, overall fidelity is substantial but incomplete, whereas relation selectivity is not reliably reproduced on the small plain-format checkpoints, where the transfer mainly reproduces the shift both questions share. Binary answer outcomes do not quantify the magnitude of the reproduced response or its shared and relation-selective components. Beyond established entity-state transfer (Geva et al., 2023; Nanda et al., 2023), target-relation sources substantially narrow the hidden-over-direct gap except for plain-format Gemma, and the identical relation-neutral change retains selective effects that depend on the receiving question, beyond random and other-replacement controls. Which changes to inject. Aligned changes on all rows beat entity rows alone at 50% depth (Section 4.2) and, on five of six checkpoints, the best tested single vectors (Section 4.3). Scaling single vectors to span-aligned row norms narrows that gap, but directions, coverage and prefix information also vary, so row structure is not isolated.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: With known answer prefixes supplied, entity-replacement responses are partly portable across questions: other-relation hidden reuse removes 3851% of the no-change error on plain-format Qwen and Llama and 5869% on Gemma with BOS restored, with formatand cohort-dependent exceptions. On the small checkpoints in the original plain format, other-relation hidden reuse mainly reproduces the shared shift without reliably lowering relation-selective error. The identical relation-neutral change can nevertheless produce selective effects that depend on the receiving question. With the three cohorts pooled, target-relation sources substantially narrow the hidden-over-direct advantage except for plain-format Gemma; the residual advantage is unconfirmed and not replacement-specific. Span-aligned addition beats the best tested single vectors on five of six checkpoints, four under pooled correction. Together, these measurements quantify the magnitude, relation selectivity and construction dependence of cross-question response reuse. 9 Cross-Prompt Response Reuse PREPRINT

sections.title: 7 Limitations
sections.content: Relation labels and question wording vary together, and some labels express overlapping predicates, so they do not isolate semantic relation from wording. The fresh cohorts test new replacements within largely familiar relation and template families (Appendix B). Eligibility requires equal-length token-span replacements in English questions or completion prompts. Results cover six instruct checkpoints from three families, with size and training lineage confounded. Chat jointly changes the template, BOS token, answer instruction and scored terminator (end-of-turn token instead of newline). Restoring BOS alone reproduces Gemmas chat-format improvement but not Llama-3.2-1Bs chat-format selectivity gain, whose source among the other components is unresolved. The three answer comparisons were not tested for Llama with BOS, and fresh cohorts were not run in chat format. Confirmatory studies use one interface at 50% depth. The descriptive answer depth and position scans reuse the observed 35-block cohort and split constructions by target rows; their target-relation row subsets and neutral-source runs lack Qwen2.5-7B, whose re-run failed its consistency check (Appendix E). Suffix interpolation is inexact at the decoder input and lets entity rows receive non-entity source rows. Span-aligned addition applies only to same-replacement sources; different-replacement and random controls use interpolation, except in the identical-content experiment, whose other-replacement control interpolates within the entity span (Appendix G). Attention knockouts locate attention paths rather than heads or features and also shift the unedited answer contrast. Construction comparisons jointly vary coverage, direction and prefix information and do not evaluate behavioral steering; norm-matched vectors borrow span-aligned norms (Appendix F). Complete-answer evaluation conditions sources and targets on known published-answer prefixes. Its literal candidate groups carry little absolute probability mass and exclude alternative aliases and formatting, including semantically equivalent strings (Holtzman et al., 2021); Appendix gives their masses. The next-token distribution at the answer cue and greedy generation from single capture are separate measures: one question-plus-cue capture with other-relation sources reproduced the edited greedy answer string for only 523% of targets (Appendix E). Component splits are algebraic output contrasts, not identified hidden-state mechanisms. The protocols were internal, not externally registered, and fixed confirmatory comparisons before their own outcomes. Later designs used earlier findings and materials, including the choice of other-relation sources, the BOS ablations after Gemmas plain-format failures, and the 90-construction comparison, whose distinct selection and evaluation cohorts had all been studied before. Appendix B.5 gives the order and scope of each protocol. The neutral-source controls use two fixed English templates, and the different-replacement control changes both the original and replacement entity. Sign inference assumes independent blocks or relation/template components. Grouping recorded overlaps leaves possible dependence through aliases, recurring answers and relation labels reused across cohorts. Label resampling shows sensitivity for some mean effects and positive-block shares but gives descriptive intervals, not dependenceadjusted family-wise tests (Appendix C). Study-wide Holm correction addresses separate multiplicity question and changes 26 conclusions, including first-fresh-cohort selectivity and some tuned-vector and identical-content results; Llama-3.1-8Bs second-cohort selectivity replication remains  (Table 25)  . Limited power also precludes interpreting failed comparisons as equivalence (Appendix C). constant push would also pass the fresh-cohort selectivity sign tests, so interpretation relies on magnitudes and different-replacement comparisons  (Table 24)  .

sections.content: B.1 Blocks and eligibility Each answer-study block crosses two factual entity replacements with two queried relations and six published ZsRE question templates: two sources and one target per relation. Replacements preserve token length on all three tokenizers and change at least two entity-overlapping tokens. Source and target contexts diverge before the entity. Within each cohort, relation labels, entity identities and known aliases, templates and complete inputs are disjoint across blocks; this does not make cohorts independent of one another. The introductory example and Table 5 come from block 11 of the earlier 40-block crossing, selected retrospectively for readable wording, not its outcomes. They are not examples selected from the 35-block answer cohort. The earlier next-token cohorts and their inference units are summarized in Appendix B.4. Table 5: Six published question templates in one complete block. Substitute with each endpoint of SLIB to JDeveloper and Apache Derby to OpenLayers. The entity slot is the only replacement in the displayed wording. Relation label Role Published question developer developer developer programming language programming language programming language By whom was developed? Source 1 Source 2 Which company developed x? Target Source 1 What is the programming language for x? Source 2 What programming language was used to write x? Target Which programming language is written in? What is the name of xs developer? B.2 Answer cohorts and overlap The original answer cohort has 35 disjoint four-target blocks, 70 labels, 140 distinct entities and 210 templates. It separates targetand other-relation new-answer strings on all 140 targets, with no recorded dependency edges. Of the 70 relations and 210 templates, 68 and 202 recur from the crossing, and 67 and 197 recur from the native-amplitude study. These are again new-entity rather than new-family materials. Each targets candidates include published answers for both original and replacement entities under both relations; only the replacements groups AT and AO enter the contrast, and the New-first and In-set summaries use the full candidate set (Tables 23 and 29). There are 532 target/candidate pairs per checkpoint, at most six candidates per target. All sources, clean target states and predictions are frozen for each checkpoint before edited-target answers are measured. The two fresh cohorts contain 33 and 31 further four-target blocks. They reuse 64 of 66 and 62 of 62 relation labels and 192 of 198 and 185 of 186 templates from earlier cohorts. Thus they assess new entities within largely familiar relation and wording families, not new-family generalization. Selection excludes the earlier cohorts entities, aliases and complete inputs, retains equal-length, tokenizer-compatible replacements, and uses the same block and answer-group construction. Only the input rendering and scored terminator change across formats (Appendix A). B.3 Artifacts, data and computation Checkpoints and input formats. The fixed released checkpoints are Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024), hidden state 12 of 24 (dimension 896); Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (Meta, 2024), state 8 of 16 (dimension 2,048); and Gemma-2-2B-it (Gemma Team, 2024), state 13 of 26 (dimension 2,304), each at 50% depth, the interface at which changes are injected. scale replication uses the same-family Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024), Llama-3.18B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024) and Gemma-2-9B-it (Gemma Team, 2024), at states 14 of 28, 16 of 32 and 21 of 42; their tokenizers are byte-identical to the small checkpoints, so the answer inputs are unchanged. Original studies use plain raw text without special tokens, fixed before outcomes: no chat template or Llama/Gemma beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, although both tokenizers add one by default. The first token acts as an attention sink (Xiao et al., 2024); without it, one-token perturbations spread further (Barbero et al., 2025) and Gemma-2 loses its massive activations and degrades (Owen et al., 2025). Later protocols add each checkpoints chat template and plain text with only the BOS token restored (plain+BOS). The testbed, steering-completion and identical-content studies use each checkpoints default encoding, plain for Qwen, whose tokenizer adds no BOS token, and plain+BOS for Llama and Gemma. The checkpoints are used under their published terms: Apache 2.0 for Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, the Qwen Research License, which permits non-commercial research use, for Qwen2.53B-Instruct, the Llama 3.2 and Llama 3.1 Community Licenses for Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, 17 Cross-Prompt Response Reuse PREPRINT and the Gemma Terms of Use for both Gemma-2 checkpoints. Materials come from public research releases of ZsRE, BEAR, T-REx (as distributed with LPAQA), ParaRel and LPAQA, and from public Wikidata metadata. They state facts about named public entities, including birth dates, family members and party membership; no new personal data are collected. All prompts and answers are English. All model runs use CPUs, float32 model weights and float64 scoring, with Python 3.12.9, PyTorch 2.13.0 (Paszke et al., 2019), Transformers 5.14.1 (Wolf et al., 2020) and NumPy 2.5.1 (Harris et al., 2020). The small, 1.5B and 3B checkpoints run with eight threads; the larger checkpoints run as four 48-thread processes per 192-core node. An earlier descriptive answer standard-patch extension on the original cohort, not analysed here, and all 7B, 8B and 9B runs use the official PyTorch 2.13.0+cpu build and the other measurements the macOS arm64 wheel of the same version, with the same scientific settings and the 103 logit replay check: every continuation from an unpatched interface must reproduce the clean logits within 103. We plan to release the code, block and candidate identifiers, saved predictions, run records and written protocols; text derived from ZsRE and LPAQA will be released only as their terms permit. BEAR is released under CC BY-SA 4.0, the ParaRel repository under MIT, and Wikidata structured metadata under CC0.1 We could not establish an explicit license for the exact ZsRE release or for LPAQAs prompt files and bundled T-REx training subset from their release pages.2 Public availability is not treated as redistribution license; reuse must retain upstream attribution and resolve these terms before repackaging those materials. The four earlier next-token cohorts and the original answer cohort total 2,076 target/checkpoint evaluations on the small checkpoints; the two fresh cohorts add 256 new targets, while auxiliary studies reuse some targets. The answer standard-patch extension used 23.52 allocated core-hours plus 3.89 for an incomplete launch. The depth/scale, span-aligned-scan/chat/first-fresh-cohort, BOS/neutral/second-cohort, testbed/depth, steering-completion and identicalcontent studies used, respectively, about 3, 8, 6.5, 14.3, 4.3 and 1.8 reported CPU hours for the smaller-checkpoint runs, and 448, 1,020, 1,178, 3,293, 889 and 404 allocated core-hours for the larger checkpoints. The span-aligned-scan group also used 11.6 allocated core-hours in an incomplete launch; its smaller-checkpoint figure includes the auxiliary descriptive 1.5B and 3B runs, whose outcomes are not analysed here. CPU time and allocated core-hours are distinct quantities; we did not record project-wide total and do not infer one from target counts. Saved-data checks run no models. This work is intended for controlled analysis of response transfer, not deployment of factual edits. Public named-entity facts can still be sensitive, outdated or biased; identities are retained because entity replacement is the research variable, not because the records are anonymous. We performed no dedicated offensive-content audit and collected no new participant data. Response reuse could propagate false personal claims or be misused to manipulate answers. The English-only selection and limited checkpoints also preclude population-level fairness claims. B.4 Earlier next-token studies Four studies preceding the answer evaluation measured next-token logit changes immediately after the input prompt, without an answer cue or BOS token; the multi-token study included 132 complete questions and 52 completion prompts among its 184 edits. They used the three small checkpoints and public ZsRE, BEAR, T-REx, ParaRel and LPAQA materials (Wiland et al., 2024; Elsahar et al., 2018; Elazar et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2020). B.5 Study sequence The independent single-token, multi-token, 40-block crossing and native-amplitude studies preceded the 35-block answer study. An earlier 157-pair pilot is not evidence: its pair-level tests assumed independence despite recurring subjects and relations. Its identities, aliases and prompts are excluded from later selections. The pilot fixed the 50% interface; the later descriptive all-layer scan on the crossing cohort did not retune it. Each core study had an internal written protocol before its edited-target outcomes, not an external registration. Later designs were informed by earlier findings: the answer study chose other-relation sources after the crossing cohorts descriptive answer comparison separated the routes most clearly. With target-relation sources, the descriptive route-gap intervals included zero on Llama and Gemma. After the plain-format answer and scale studies came the span-aligned depth scan, chat format and the first fresh cohort. That cohorts two pre-specified selectivity tests followed up the descriptive reductions on Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B. BOS ablation, neutral sources and the second fresh cohort followed Gemmas known plain-format failures.
